title: Inishrush, Dunaghy & Drumragh collateral leads
standfirst: Family-register, census, tithe and marriage evidence places several Glasgow-associated households around Inishrush. The records illuminate a neighbourhood and possible collateral paths, not a joined Lisnagaver pedigree.
question: Can Inishrush, Dunaghy and Drumragh records establish a documented bridge to the later Rasharkin households?
answer: John born in 1767 is probably the 1831 Inishrush householder, but no Irish record names his parents. Adam, born about 1758, cannot be his father; brotherhood or cousinship remains possible. A later marriage makes the James in John’s 1847 letter a strong identification, while still not proving that younger Adam was Adam Glasgow-3902 or that this group was kin to Lisnagaver.

chapters.title: John, Mary and the Inishrush household
body: John and Mary Arthur’s family Bible records their 1798 marriage and nine children. The close fit between that family and the 1831 Inishrush house makes the repeated identity probable, not certain.
The Bible is strong family evidence but does not name John's parents. Its naming pattern makes older Adam and Maria useful search names only.

chapters.title: A letter points to a later marriage
body: John's 1847 letter relayed that James Glasgow had a child by a servant who was Henry Barkly's daughter. The 1851 marriage of James, farmer of Inishrush and son of Adam, to Rosanna Barkley of Tyanee closely matches those particulars.
The child is unnamed, and this does not establish that James's father was Adam Glasgow-3902.

chapters.title: Dunaghy, Drumragh and Rasharkin
body: The 1825 tithe list records Robert Glasco at Dunbught and two distinct James Glasgows at Ballybogey; 'junior' alone does not prove father and son. A 1828 marriage identifies Mary Glasgow of Drumragh in the wider area.
Maria Glasgow's documented Wallace children were born at Rasharkin in 1840 and 1842. That places one Inishrush descendant branch beside Lisnagaver, without proving kinship.

clusters.title: John and Mary Arthur
clusters.summary: Bible, locality and household evidence strongly support John-822 as the Inishrush-associated John.
clusters.boundary: No record names his parents; the pending duplicate identity is not a proved merge.

clusters.title: James and the Barkley connection
clusters.summary: The 1851 marriage closely fits the James and Barkley details in John’s 1847 letter.
clusters.boundary: It does not identify the unnamed child or prove older Adam's identity.

clusters.title: Neighbouring collateral occurrences
clusters.summary: Tithe and marriage records identify several named local occurrences and a Rasharkin descendant movement.
clusters.boundary: They do not establish links among the households or to Lisnagaver.

links.label: 1847 letter and 1851 marriage share names, setting and Barkley detail
shared district network; no stated kinship

proved: John and Mary's recorded family-register dates.
supported: John-822 is probably the 1831 Inishrush householder.
The letter's James is likely the 1851 groom.
hypothesis: John and Adam were brothers or cousins.
Older Adam and Maria were their parents.
unresolved: A bridge to Lisnagaver or Bann Valley.

gaps.why: It may preserve sources for John’s parents and descendants.

gaps.title: Separate the Ballybogey Jameses
gaps.why: A succession record could turn a label into a stated relationship.

gaps.title: Inspect first Lisnagaver leases
gaps.why: They could test, not assume, movement into the later settlement.
